title: Fold an outlet's three stiff copper wires back into its wall box and seat the outlet
instruction: Put the outlet back in its wall box, ready for its screws, with every wire inside the box. Then let go.
context: Putting a receptacle back in its box is routine for electricians (O*NET 47-2111.00, 821,000 US jobs in 2025: "Assemble, install, test, or maintain electrical or electronic wiring, equipment, appliances, apparatus, or fixtures, using hand tools or power tools") and general maintenance and repair workers (49-9071.00, 1,621,800 jobs: "Assemble, install, or repair wiring, electrical or electronic components, pipe systems, plumbing, machinery, or equipment"). The wires are solid 12 AWG copper: they keep whatever bend they are given and push back. Pushed straight in, their loops stand up over the box's top edge and are trapped between the outlet and the wall, where a pinched conductor is a shock and fire risk. Each loop has to be folded into the box while the other hand holds the outlet, and only then will the outlet go home. No screws are driven: the task ends with the outlet let go, sitting where its screws would reach.
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table: x forward (away from the robot), y to the robot's left; heights above the table. Wall (fixed, off-white board): 32 cm wide, 30 cm tall, 1.27 cm thick, standing on the table with its front face at x 37.5, from y -24 to y +8. Wall box (fixed, blue plastic, open to the front, its rim flush with the wall's face): inside 5.2 cm wide, 9.0 cm tall and 6.6 cm deep, walls 2.5 mm thick, opening centred at y -8, 19 cm up. Inside it, on the centre line, a screw boss 1.0 cm wide stands 0.67 cm in from the top wall and another from the bottom wall; their screw holes are 8.33 cm apart. Outlet (loose, 70 g): a steel mounting strap 3.35 cm wide, 10.67 cm tall and 1.5 mm thick; an ivory plastic body 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 2.0 cm deep behind the strap; an ivory face 3.35 cm wide, 6.8 cm tall and 0.45 cm thick in front of it. It hangs on its wires, upright, facing the robot, centred on the opening, with the back of its strap 11.5 cm in front of the wall. Wires (three, solid 12 AWG copper, conductor 2.05 mm across): one black and one white, insulated to 3.0 mm across, each 20.0 cm long, and one bare, 18.9 cm long. All three come from one point at the top back of the box, 5.8 cm behind the wall's face and 3 cm above the opening's centre. The black wire ends on the right side of the outlet's body and the white wire on its left side, both 1.2 cm above the outlet's centre; the bare wire ends on the left side, 3.0 cm below the centre. Each wire has two old folds about 9 mm high left in it and runs in a shallow arch from the box to the outlet. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Measured on the last step from the outlet's pose, 20 or 21 points along each wire, and the grippers' positions. Score 0 unless all of these hold: the outlet is upright (its long axis within 15 degrees of vertical); every corner of its strap is within 15 mm of the wall's face (near enough for a 1 in mounting screw to reach its hole); every wire is inside the box (no point of a wire more than 2 mm in front of the wall's face, apart from the end fixed to the outlet's terminal, which is part of the outlet; and no point outside the opening's outline within 3 mm of the face); and the outlet has been let go (the grip centre and pad tips of both grippers at least 3 cm from the outlet and from every wire, with the outlet moving under 1 cm/s, for the last 2 s). Then: 1.0 if both of the strap's screw holes are within 3 mm of the box's screw holes, measured across the wall; 0.5 if either is further off. Doing nothing, a push that leaves a wire trapped or showing, and an outlet still held or pressed in place all score 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed, but copper keeps its bends. Pull the outlet back out until the back of its strap is 11.5 cm in front of the wall, and re-dress each wire to its starting arch with its two old folds (a bending jig, or a fresh length of wire).
fidelity: Each wire is a chain of rigid links 10.7 mm long on two-axis joints that bend like solid 12 AWG copper: stiffness from E 117 GPa, first yield at 59 N mm, and work hardening from annealed copper's stress-strain curve, so a bend stays and gets harder to bend further. Twist along a wire and stretch are left out. The outlet, box and wall are rigid and true size.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0 after 2,400 steps (termination: step limit); scripted demo: 1.0 after 1,352 steps (termination: success)
